title: The wheel of the world
hook: the seekers describe what they saw: the world as one wheel, spun by nature's three strands around God at the hub
carry: nature turns the wheel; god holds the hub
tomorrow: a swan flies into the wheel

segments.voice: Yesterday: one Lord behind time, fate and chance. None of them alone was enough, and in meditation the seekers saw the power of God.
screen: `ONE LORD BEHIND TIME, FATE AND CHANCE.`

segments.voice: Look at a bicycle wheel long enough and it starts to look like an argument. One rim. A hub that barely moves. Dozens of spokes pulling against each other, and the whole thing works only because the tension is shared. Spin it and the spokes blur. Stop it and you can count them again. The sages of the Shvetashvatara looked at the world and saw something like that. Not a ladder, not a pyramid. A wheel. And today's verse does a strange thing with it: it counts the parts.
screen: `ONE RIM, ONE HUB, MANY SPOKES.` → `SPIN IT: A BLUR.` → `STOP IT: COUNT THE PARTS.`

segments.voice: Now the seekers describe what they saw, and verse 1.4 is almost a riddle. They see the Lord as a wheel with one rim, three tires, sixteen ends, fifty spokes, twenty counter-spokes, six sets of eight, one rope of many forms, three paths, and one delusion with two causes. Read it once and it's a parts list. Read it with the old commentators and it becomes a map. The one rim is usually read as nature itself, prakriti, the stuff everything is made of. The sixteen ends are often counted as the five elements plus the eleven powers of body and mind. The fifty spokes, in the commentaries, are fifty states of mind, matching a list known from the school called Samkhya. Scholars still argue over some of these numbers, and the Upanishad never explains them. Then verse 1.5 turns the wheel into a river with fifty kinds of grief. But the three tires carry one of Hinduism's most used ideas: the three gunas, the strands of nature. Sattva, brightness. Rajas, restlessness. Tamas, heaviness. Food, weather, a mood: all woven from the three. Families still call a meal sattvic, or a slammed-door week all rajas. And here's the teaching: the strands belong to the wheel, to nature. At the hub, the Upanishad says, is the power of God who turns it. Many teachers draw the lesson the Bhagavad Gita makes plain later: the strands spin, and the self only watches. So a restless week is the wheel turning, not the whole of who you are.
screen: `ONE RIM, THREE TIRES, SIXTEEN ENDS.` · `THE OLD MAP: NATURE, POWERS, STATES OF MIND.` · `SATTVA, RAJAS, TAMAS.` · then, large: `NATURE TURNS THE WHEEL. GOD HOLDS THE HUB.`

segments.voice: Picture a wheel, slowly turning, and notice your own spokes as they pass: a thought, a sound, an itch, a plan. Give each one a strand as it goes by, bright, restless or heavy, without judging it. When you lose track, start again. For the last few breaths, rest at the center, the part of you that has been watching the strands go by all along.
The wheel. The Shvetashvatara's picture of the turning world: one rim, three strands, many spokes, all moving around a center that doesn't move.
Your line: nature turns the wheel; God holds the hub. Tomorrow, a swan flies into the wheel. See you there.

notes: Readings of 1.4 vary: 'one rim' as prakriti or maya; 'sixteen ends' as five elements plus eleven organs (or the sixteen vikaras); 'fifty spokes' as the fifty pratyayas of Samkhya (viparyaya, ashakti, tushti, siddhi). Confirm the readings the Keeper prefers.
The list of features ('six sets of eight, one rope of many forms, three paths, one delusion with two causes') follows Müller/Hume renderings; please check.
Gunas glossed as brightness, restlessness and heaviness (sattva, rajas, tamas).

Reviewer softened 'borrowed from the school called Samkhya' to 'matching a list known from' Samkhya, and the trapdoor's 'encodes' to 'is often read as encoding': whether a classical Samkhya system existed before this Upanishad, or the two grew together, is debated.
